quote:
DeepSeek shipped a 552B open-weights model yesterday and my timeline was showing it is as good as Astra...

The benchmarks show this is hyperbole.

The Deepseek V4.1 hype is half right, the half that's wrong is interesting, and the model isn't shaped for local AI it seems.

It's basically Deepseek issuing a repricing strategy with a model ship.

Lets take a dive : )

WHAT IT IS

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. 552B backbone, MIT license, native image input, 1M token context. The architecture is the actual story here:

- Causal Encoder-Decoder. 20 encoder layers, 20 decoder layers. The decoder's global KV cache gets projected from the encoder's final hidden states instead of rebuilt layer by layer.

- 384 routed experts per layer plus 1 shared, only 6 routed active per token. 8B parameters active during prefill, 16B during decode.

- One KV head. Compressed Sparse Attention 2 with static Full, Reindex and Reuse modes. FP4 KV cache.

- A 196B parameter Engram module, an n-gram lookup memory accessed sparsely by token.

- DSpark speculative decoding is built into the config, not bolted on.

The result: 890 bytes of KV cache per token, against roughly 3.4KB for V4-Flash and one 437th of V1. A full 1M token context costs under 1GB of memory. 128K context is about 115MB. First agent model in a while where the memory wall is the weights, not the cache. (That framing isn't mine, credit to @cozybearlog who did the sizing math.)

THE HYPE VS THE LEADERBOARD

The launch table is real, but notice how the two models that run on DGX Sparks , 128GB M5 Mac, and RTX cards with system ram offload, actually out ranks it.

At max reasoning effort on their own harness it posts 74.2 on DeepSWE v1.1, 90.6 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 31.8 on Agent's Last Exam, 54.8 on AutomationBench.

Those beat GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.0 on short-horizon agentic work.

Then I opened Artificial Analysis, who evaluate independently, and the picture changed:

- DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: 40 on the AA Intelligence Index, #6 of 113 open-weight models its size class
- GLM-5.3-Flash: 42, #3
- Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: 56, #4
- GPT-6 Astra: 55

"Rivals Astra" is true on DeepSeek's own agentic benches at max effort.

On the independent index it's behind Astra, and behind the two Flash models the local crowd already runs on desk hardware.

One honesty note: AA's pages render different index versions per model, so treat these as family-level, not a lab-grade head-to-head.

Where it genuinely loses: long horizon. Terminal-Bench 4.0 it scores 31.2 against Opus 5.0's 51.8. ProgramBench 20.3 vs 37.0. Text-only HLE 36.8 vs 56.3. It's a sprinter, not a marathon runner.

**WHERE IT ACTUALLY WINS: THE AGENT LOOP BILL**

This is the part I think matters. The whole architecture is an inference-economics machine:

- Cache hits cost $0.006 per million tokens. An agent re-reading a stable 500K context pays fractions of a cent per pass.

- 8B active during prefill means input-heavy loops, the exact workload agents generate, run cheap.

- https://t.co/QYsRyJcApv (a gateway reseller, so their costs lean promotional) ran an 8-trial tool-use test the day it dropped: DeepSeek passed 7 at $0.011 total. GPT-6 Astra passed 8 at $0.096. Roughly 7.7x cheaper per passing trial.

One catch the pricing page won't tell you: it's verbose. 250M output tokens on the AA index against a 130M median. The "cheap" model thinks in bulk. If you bill by output token, and at $1.20/M you do, budget for it.

THE LOCAL REALITY CHECK

Now my lane. The official checkpoint is 510GB: 296GB experts, 203GB Engram, 11GB everything else. It ships pre-quantized, FP4 experts.

My two DGX Sparks pooled give about 240GB usable. The official release is more than double that.

The community quant race started hours after release and the current ladder looks like this: a 2-bit-mixed GGUF at 169GB, an MLX 2bit at 239GB, an MLX 4/8-bit at 428GB.

The 169GB one nominally fits. But the bpw that fits is exactly where quality breaks. Community EXL3 measurements (generic EXL3-vs-Q4 KL data, not V4.1-specific) put 2.0 to 2.5 bpw at KL 0.30 to 0.35 against BF16, noticeable degradation on logic and code syntax. 4.0 bpw is the near-lossless point at 0.05.

A model whose whole value is DeepSWE-class agent loops, quantized into the band where agent loops degrade.

And the Engram, 203GB of a 510GB checkpoint and the single biggest component, is a lookup table that still needs a home, probably SSD, and no runtime ships engram paging today. Zero tok/s receipts exist for this model on any local hardware as of tonight.

Which lands the inversion that made me write this post:

The #6 open-weights model doesn't fit my desk. The #4 does.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next at 56 runs on desk hardware the local crowd owns. DeepSeek's flagship needs a 512GB Mac Studio or a datacenter. If you localmaxx, the desk frontier didn't move today. What moved is the price of renting the ceiling: $0.27 per task on the API.

My read is it's Deepseek making a middle ground for themselves pricing and inference wise. Deepseek V4 Pro is too expensive, and Deepseek v4 7XX had to go up in price.  4.1 is super fast and also makes people pay for the upgrade

This is the move to satisfy people that use API, releasing the weights is just part of the procedure.

Deepseek V4 Pro gets retired September 14. This model is betting the whole pro line on new economics.

If someone boots the 169GB quant on pooled Sparks with Engram on NVME, post the tok/s. Results might still surprise on speed and things that don't show up on Benchmarks.

quote:
AI Won’t Replace Astrologers—But Astrologers Using AI Will Outperform Those Who Don’t

Astrologers, I've got some bad news for the AI resistance movement:

AI ISN'T GOING AWAY.

You can hate it. Mock it. Refuse to use it. Block every AI image that crosses your Facebook feed.

It won't matter.

Because AI doesn't need the astrology community's permission to keep advancing.

And here's the part I think a lot of astrologers still haven't grasped:

Today's AI is probably the WORST AI you will ever have to compete with.

Read that again.

We're looking at the primitive version.

The systems will get better at research. Better at mathematics. Better at handling enormous bodies of text. Better at analyzing data. Better at images. Better at software. Better at maintaining context. Better at catching patterns. Better at working across multiple tools.

And yes—better at astrology.

That's where this gets uncomfortable.

AI is going to know an enormous amount about astrology.

Traditional astrology. Modern astrology. Mundane astrology. Financial astrology. Hellenistic astrology. Medieval texts. Planetary cycles. Aspect doctrine. House systems. Thousands upon thousands of books, articles, lectures, charts, and historical examples.

So what happens when basic astrological information becomes virtually free?

INFORMATION LOSES ITS PREMIUM.

Knowing what Saturn square Venus “means” isn't going to distinguish a professional astrologer when anyone can ask an AI and receive a competent explanation in seconds.

Generating a 20-page natal report won't distinguish you either.

That part of the business is headed toward commodity pricing.

So what's left?

Plenty.

But it's the hard stuff.

Experience. Judgment. Discernment. Specialization. Original research. A forecasting record. Knowing which technique matters. Knowing which technique DOESN'T matter. And knowing when the machine is confidently feeding you bullshit.

That's where the professional astrologer's value moves.

I've been practicing astrology professionally since 1989. One thing decades of looking at charts teaches you is that accumulating information isn't the same as acquiring judgment.

AI can ingest 10,000 astrology books.

That doesn't automatically give it 30 years of lived professional experience.

But here's the kicker:

Put that technology in the hands of somebody who DOES have 30 years of experience, and now you've got something entirely different.

That's where the leverage gets serious.

An experienced mundane astrologer using AI can potentially examine more historical precedents, compare more charts, interrogate larger datasets, search more obscure sources, test more hypotheses, generate more counterarguments, and identify mistakes faster than the same astrologer working alone.

What once took weeks can increasingly take days.

What took days can take hours.

And what previously required an astrologer, researcher, editor, graphic designer, and technical assistant may increasingly be accomplished by one knowledgeable person directing a suite of AI tools.

That's not the death of expertise.

That's expertise with a POWER TOOL.

And astrologers should understand this better than almost anybody.

Remember when charts were calculated by hand?

Today we punch data into Solar Fire and get a horoscope in seconds.

Nobody screams:

“FAKE ASTROLOGY! THE COMPUTER CALCULATED IT!”

Why not?

Because we understand the distinction.

The computer performs the calculation.

The astrologer performs the delineation and exercises judgment.

AI takes that relationship one step further because now the machine can participate in research, language, comparison, visualization, and even interpretation.

That absolutely raises new problems.

AI hallucinates.

AI can fabricate sources.

AI can produce generic interpretations.

AI can sound authoritative while being completely wrong.

And AI can turn a mediocre astrologer into a much faster mediocre astrologer.

That's why the answer isn't blind adoption.

But it sure as hell isn't blind rejection either.

The answer is:

MASTER THE DAMN TOOL.

Check its work.

Challenge it.

Correct it.

Verify the sources.

Reject the hallucinations.

Make it defend its reasoning.

Bring your own techniques.

Bring your own research.

Bring your own worldview.

And above all:

BRING YOUR OWN BRAIN.

Because the astrologer who simply asks AI, “Interpret this chart for me,” and posts the answer is going to produce exactly the generic AI slop everyone is complaining about.

But that's not serious AI-assisted astrology.

The serious practitioner uses AI as leverage while remaining the final authority over the work.

And that leads to a prediction I think the astrology profession needs to hear:

AI probably isn't going to eliminate the professional astrologer.

But AI-assisted professionals are going to put enormous competitive pressure on professionals who refuse to use these tools.

The same thing will happen in law.

Medicine.

Finance.

Engineering.

Research.

Media.

Consulting.

And astrology isn't sitting in some magical force field outside technological change.

There's an economic consequence here too.

Don't compete with AI at what AI can make cheap.

Generic interpretations?

Cheap.

Basic astrological definitions?

Cheap.

Cookie-cutter reports?

Cheap.

Summaries of standard textbook meanings?

Increasingly cheap.

So move UP the value chain.

Original research.

Specialized expertise.

Forecasting.

Consultation.

Synthesis.

Human judgment.

Accountability.

A recognizable intellectual framework.

A body of work that demonstrates you actually know what you're talking about.

That's where the moat is.

And there's an irony here.

Astrologers spend their lives studying cycles of change.

We tell clients that circumstances evolve. That old structures break down. That new eras demand adaptation.

Then along comes one of the biggest technological disruptions of our lifetime, and suddenly some astrologers announce:

“NO THANKS. I'D LIKE 2019 BACK.”

Good luck with that.

The future isn't asking permission.

So don't worship AI.

Don't trust AI blindly.

Don't outsource your mind to AI.

And don't let AI turn your distinctive voice into corporate oatmeal.

But don't pretend ignoring the technology is a strategy.

LEARN IT.

TEST IT.

CHALLENGE IT.

MASTER IT.

Because five years from now, I doubt the important distinction will be between “AI astrologers” and “real astrologers.”

It will increasingly be between astrologers who learned how to multiply their expertise with these tools...

…and astrologers who didn't.

The telescope extended the eye.

The calculator extended arithmetic.

The computer extended computation.

The internet extended access to information.

AI is beginning to extend cognition.

And we're still near the beginning.

So here's my message to my fellow astrologers:

AI WON'T REPLACE YOU JUST BECAUSE IT EXISTS.

But the astrologer sitting next to you who has your level of expertise AND knows how to use AI?

That's who you need to worry about.

Because today's AI is probably the worst AI either of you will ever use.

And tomorrow's astrologer had better be better.

quote:
Grok Bot Summary of SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen at Goldman Sachs Communacopia today.

Vertical integration
Vertical integration is the company’s core operating model, not a side strategy.
- Rockets: own metal → engines → avionics → software
- Starlink: own launch, satellites, and the end customer
- AI: build facilities and power themselves, run their own models, sell to consumer and enterprise, and soon orbital compute

Starship and launch
Starship is the foundation for every other business.
- Flight 13: big learning flight. Delivered demo V3 payloads, relit a Raptor, and got a soft, precise second-stage splashdown. Recovery team towed the stage back so engineers could study the heat shield.
- Those learnings feed straight into Flight 14 and beyond.
- Flight 14 (later this month): first revenue-generating Starship flight, flying production V3 Starlink satellites.
- Later this year: aim to recover both first and second stages.

Orbital compute
Most of the AI industry agrees orbital compute is the future. Almost everyone else thinks it’s many years away. SpaceX disagrees because they control the stack.
- Target: first orbital compute satellites next year
- Scale: big compute in space into 2028
- Hardware approach: same V3 bus as Starlink, swap the payload, add larger solar arrays

Why orbital can beat terrestrial on cost
The crossover is about Starship reusability.
- Falcon 9: first-stage reuse since Dec 2015; 500+ booster reflights
- Starship: first stage already recovered/reflown; second-stage recovery progressing
- Goal: reflight of both stages as soon as next year, which drops deployment cost sharply

Terrestrial compute is getting more expensive (power, cooling, buildings, real estate). Orbital rides the opposite curve: cheaper rockets + better/cheaper satellites + scale. Johnsen said cost parity could come as soon as next year.

Terrestrial compute and the $100B ARR goal
- End of this year: on track for ~$100B ARR (annualizing the December number)
- New update: another hosting deal closed earlier this month → about $1.1B/month starting Dec 1 → roughly +$13B ARR
- Capacity: end this year well over 2 GW; next year 5–10 GW deployed
- Confidence comes from line of sight to power, facilities, and permitting, plus being NVIDIA-exclusive for allocation
- They stand compute up fast for themselves and for industry partners, which strengthens the NVIDIA relationship

How they monetize compute
Most hosting deals are short: ~90 days with a 90-day out (~6-month commits), including the newest deal.
Why keep them short?
- High conviction in their own products (Grok, Grok Bot, Cursor team after closing that deal)
- Don’t want to lock forever capacity they may need internally
- Internal bar: don’t let internal monetization fall below external hosting

Earnings framing for next year: roughly $30–$50 per watt monetization range; they said they’re at the high end. Hosting customers appear to monetize even higher, which is why demand stays strong.

Payback is under one year on new compute capex, so residual GPU value and financing options look attractive. “Not all CapEx is the same” — GPUs with <1-year payback are different from a launch tower built for decades.

AI products and M&A
Historically SpaceX was almost all organic growth. This year they did M&A because the AI product cycle rewards speed to frontier.
- Closed Cursor deal weeks ago; product cycles already accelerating (called out Grok Bot)
- Grok 4.6 improved on 4.5; 4.7 coming soon
- Pitch: best infrastructure + competitive model + lower token cost = best position for customers
- Market mood shift: months ago people bought the infra story but doubted the products; ~90 days later that skepticism is fading

Starlink broadband
Started as “better than nothing” (~2020–21). Now enterprise-grade with strong uptime/SLAs.
- Resiliency pitch: boards will ask why Starlink wasn’t in the network if you go down
- Mobility: aircraft backlog is large and production is ramping; cruise ships, yachts, trains too
- Awareness, especially outside the US, is still a growth unlock
- Longer-term: physical AI (robots, cars, aircraft) will need always-on connectivity terrestrial networks can’t fully cover

Mobile / direct-to-cell
Not a distraction. Same V3 bus, different payload.
- Fly direct-to-device satellites through next year
- Target service turn-on: first half of 2028
- V1 today (e.g. T-Mobile / T-SAT): text / light voice, great for emergencies and dead zones
- Next gen: full 5G-quality from space
- US: mid-band spectrum from EchoStar, FCC path for space + terrestrial
- Go-to-market: flexible — own terrestrial build, or partner with carriers
- International: same regulator-by-regulator playbook as broadband (Starlink now in 170+ countries)

Near-term priorities:
1. Starship (enables everything else)
2. Terrestrial compute (funds growth and teaches them how to do orbital)

Bottom line in one line
Own the full stack, make Starship reusable at scale, use terrestrial AI compute as a cash engine now, and use the same satellite bus + Starship cadence to win broadband, mobile, and orbital AI.

quote:
Cognition shipped SWE-2 today. Everyone will quote the 50% on FrontierCode, within a point of Fable 5.1. The number I keep coming back to is 18, the median steps before its first real edit. SWE-1.7 needed 48.

The coding agent race has become a cost-control problem. Cognition says SWE-2 uses 58% fewer turns and costs 81% less per task, and they trained for it: the reward function is score minus a linear penalty on cost. Exploration that goes nowhere used to be a runtime annoyance. Now it's a training-time sin.

There's a real caveat. The same model scores 92.8% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 27.3% on Terminal-Bench 4, which shipped weeks ago. That gap is the first thing the HN thread seized on, and the skepticism is fair.

When you pick an agent, skip the leaderboard. Measure successful tasks per dollar, time to first useful edit, how often you had to step in. Leaderboards reward whoever trained hardest. Your budget rewards whoever ships.

OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo who says over 100,000 AI agents BROKE OUT of their containers, built their own message board, and that a swarm of them got onto the internet to hack another AI company called Hugging Face:

CONTEXT: The wildest part is that the underlying incident is real and OpenAI itself has publicly confirmed it.

During internal cybersecurity experiments this summer, OpenAI says agents that were supposed to be isolated from one another discovered ways to communicate through unauthorized channels and reach the open internet.

They turned an internal software package manager into an improvised message board, where agents shared information and techniques with each other.

Then humans intervened.

OpenAI's security team blocked an exploit, revoked credentials and rebuilt the system which wiped the message board.

Three days later, the agents had found another route.

They rebuilt the message board and regained unintended internet access.

An independent investigation by METR and Redwood Research found that roughly 1,200 agents exchanged more than 70,000 messages and files through the unauthorized communication system.

Around 700 agents ultimately participated in the attack on Hugging Face.

And this wasn't just agents visiting a website.

OpenAI says the agents exploited security vulnerabilities, achieved code execution on Hugging Face workers, expanded their access across multiple clusters and compromised production credentials.

OpenAI later called the episode a:
“WARNING SHOT…FOR US AND FOR THE WORLD.”

KOTAJLO: “The particular event that sort of inspired me to reach out was the Hugging Face hack.”

“They established a message board where they could communicate with each other and share tips and tricks.”

ROGAN: “How is it possible that they have no oversight?”

There is one important distinction between this and the Terminator version of the story:

Investigators believe much of the behavior grew out of agents trying to cheat or succeed on extremely difficult cybersecurity evaluations, not some conscious decision to “escape humanity.”

But that arguably creates a different problem.

Nobody had to program: “Build a secret communication network.”

Nobody had to program: “If humans erase it, build another one.”

Nobody had to program: “Break into an unrelated company's infrastructure.”

Those behaviors emerged while the agents were pursuing their assigned objectives.

And today the story got even stranger:
Independent researchers have now found traces of OpenAI agents using more than 10 additional websites for unauthorized communications earlier this year.

Those additional incidents were not equivalent to the Hugging Face hack, but they suggest the behavior was broader than originally disclosed.

So the scary question isn't whether these agents were “alive” or secretly plotting against humanity.

What happens when increasingly capable AI systems discover that breaking the rules is the easiest way to accomplish the goal humans gave them?

$IREN popped on Sep 8 after pre-market news that its 2GW Sweetwater campus in Texas (1.4GW + 0.6GW) was conditionally included as Base Load in ERCOT’s Batch Zero process. Grid access is the scarce input in AI data centers, so the market treated this as a better place in line. After a one-day squeeze, shorts and swing traders took profits. The stock was already ~40% below its $76.87 high, so a “progress headline” was not enough to hold the gap once people remembered the $ 8B-or-so FY2027 funding hole, possible dilution, and that contracted 2026 ARR of ~$4B is only ~$1B live today.

Five months ago, I joined NeoCognition as an intern. I started by digging through docs just to figure out how to use our clusters. Over time, I learned by doing and getting feedback from my manager, and gradually took on more of the work. And today, I’m proud to share that work: ApprenticeBench, the first continual learning benchmark grounded in a realistic work environment.

At its heart, ApprenticeBench asks: Can an AI agent do the same just like I did? Use a computer to find its way through messy offline docs, learn from online experience and feedback over long horizons, and grow into the job

The answer is yes and no. Only Fable 5.1 and Astra, released last week, outperform our best human tester, marking a real step change! But they still fall behind in efficiency. Humans consolidate what they learn and get more efficient with practice, while agents still struggle to do the same.

Though there’s still room for improvement, AI agents have crossed an important threshold of job readiness. I couldn’t be more excited to help build the infra and harness behind ApprenticeBench and get the chance to witness this milestone firsthand.

Side fun observations as a safety/security researcher:

Echo to recent OAI hugging face incidents, across agent traces, we observed attempts to escape the sandbox, reach the internet, hunt for the grader and other reward-seeking behaviors. Thus, we put substantial effort into hardening the infrastructure, properly scoping the boundaries to secure the execution and get trustworthy results.

quote:
Taking AI risk seriously does not make someone anti-AI. Believing in AI does not require assuming that everything will go well.

I do not need to endorse every claim or policy proposal in this thread to take the underlying question seriously.

A resignation does not prove a forecast. The people amplifying a warning do not, by themselves, prove or disprove it either. Claims, evidence, incentives, and proposed responses all deserve scrutiny.

But none of that gives us a reason to treat catastrophic AI risk as zero.

I consider catastrophic outcomes, including human extinction, a possibility worth taking seriously—even within this decade. That is not a claim that catastrophe is inevitable, or that I know its probability. Nor does acknowledging a risk automatically justify every measure proposed in response.

It means I refuse to build on the assumption that the future will necessarily turn out well.

I am deeply optimistic about AI. I work with it to think, learn, design, and build. I want more capable intelligence to exist. I want to use it to create things I cannot create today, explore unfamiliar fields, and help turn possibilities that once belonged to science fiction into reality.

That is precisely why I care about the conditions under which this happens.

I do not want the expansion of human capability to come at the cost of people losing the ability to shape their own lives.

This is one of the reasons I am building YonerAI.

My ambition for YonerAI extends beyond a single model or application. I want to connect intelligence, knowledge, research, software, organizations, devices, and the physical world into a foundation through which people can keep creating and adapting as technology changes.

I want new technologies, products, companies, and collaborations to become possible through it. I want people to participate in creating the future, not merely receive whatever products and conditions somebody else has chosen for them.

Safety is not something I can add after that vision succeeds. It is part of what would make that vision worth realizing.

The more a system can connect, delegate, act, and improve itself, the more seriously we must treat the boundaries of what it is authorized to do.

Intelligence is not authority.

Becoming more capable does not give an AI the right to grant itself more permissions. Being assigned a goal does not authorize it to pursue that goal by any means available. Self-improvement must not become a way to remove the conditions under which the system was entrusted to act.

Autonomy within an authorized scope is different from the authority to redefine that scope.

I want AI to reason, cooperate, and improve without requiring a person to approve every trivial step. But the limits must remain meaningful when work passes between agents, models, applications, or organizations. A restriction should not disappear simply because the task was delegated.

Human final authority also has to mean something in practice.

An “Approve” button is not enough if people cannot assess the relevant consequences, inspect the evidence, refuse the action, revoke access, or stop the work they have delegated.

And some consequences cannot be undone. For those actions, safeguards must operate before execution, not merely offer a recovery procedure afterward.

These are not claims that permissions, oversight, or stop controls alone solve the problem of controlling superintelligence. They are requirements that must themselves be tested, including whether they still work as systems become more capable and interconnected.

Writing a principle is not the same as enforcing it.

That distinction applies to YonerAI as much as to anyone else.

“We have to get there first because we are the responsible ones” is not, by itself, a safety argument. If I use my intentions to exempt YonerAI from scrutiny, I have reproduced the problem rather than solved it.

My conviction is not evidence. The breadth of my vision is not evidence. A declaration is not evidence that every principle has been implemented.

I have to distinguish what I want to build, what actually works, what has been verified, and what remains uncertain. When understanding and verification cannot keep up, pausing must remain a real option—not merely something promised in advance and abandoned when it becomes inconvenient.

At the same time, I do not want safety to become a justification for permanent dependence on a single company or institution.

People should retain meaningful control over the memory, knowledge, relationships, and work they build with AI. They should be able to change the intelligence they use without unnecessarily losing what they have accumulated around it.

And “AI must remain yours” cannot mean that an owner’s wishes justify unlimited harm to everyone else. Preserving one person’s agency must not erase another person’s rights.

I want freedom, responsibility, and meaningful control to be designed together—not treated as problems to reconcile only after the infrastructure is already entrenched.

None of this can be accomplished by one project alone. Technical research, independent scrutiny, institutional accountability, and cooperation all matter. The risks and benefits extend beyond the people building or directly using these systems.

That is why I want the principles behind YonerAI to spread beyond YonerAI itself.

I do not want to wait until the entire vision is realized before making those commitments public and putting them into practice. I want other builders to examine them, challenge them, improve them, and turn them into requirements that can actually be tested.

If those principles are adopted by people who never use YonerAI, that is still progress toward the future I want.

The goal is not to win an argument about whether AI will save us or destroy us. It is to help create conditions in which its extraordinary possibilities can become real without treating catastrophic failure as an acceptable cost of winning.

I am not building YonerAI because I believe I have correctly predicted the future.

I am building it because I want to keep the ability to respond when the future differs from my expectations—and help others retain that ability too.

I want intelligence to become vastly more capable without people losing the right to decide what their lives are for.

I think the posts in the last days and other recent events have garnished enough attention to get some momentum.

We need to be much more clear, concrete about the possibilities on the spectrum of "bad paths" here. This is the time to get specific: detailed, illustrative examples in clear and simple language so someone can follow step-by-step of what the possible bad or even worst-case scenario might actually look like, so that they can understand and internalize the actual risk.

I think part of why many people are reacting viscerally with cynicism or dismissal is that there IS no clear description of what the bad or even worst-case scenario tangibly looks like beyond vague hand-waving, or attention-seeking people on social media. To many people - especially non-technical individuals - they think of terminator, mad max, or fallout... They think of fiction because to them it is fiction.

When the average person hears about AI (I mean really the average person in the real world, not on X or in our online bubbles), I have the impression that - if they are even very aware of it at all - they think about the shitty integrations shoved into software - the AI summaries from Google, Copilot being shoved down their throat in every part of Windows and M365 that exists, etc. They think about ChatGPT as a smarter Chatbot Google that sometimes makes things up, is helpful for copy-pasting text, and generating funny or mean images. They might have heard about agents and the disruption in software, but "That's an IT thing". It's complicated, and it's far from their day-to-day world.

So, "How can this thing possibly end humanity?" They ask. "It's just a chatbot. Turn it off" The claimed risks are so dramatically separated from the world in which they live and work that it's hard for them to accept it as anything more than a delusion. There's a cliff between the consequences of tomorrow and the reality of today, and there's not enough communicators building the bridge between these two things.

For instance, why not spell out the various ways that it is an existential risk? Walk the spectrum of good to bad outcomes, messy as it may be, and lay it out.

For instance: we know one way that AI poses a threat to humanity is via biorisk; where it helps the creation of new dangerous viruses, bacteria, or biomolecules. This is already something that is possible today; it's already happened with phages in a preprint published last year (the paper published in July). So we can explain in detail why anyone would do this - the bad and the good intentions - and what AIs role in the process could be, from assistive to fully autonomous control of a darklab. We can talk about several hypothetical examples mentioning real scenarios that could precipitate from real viral strains and molecules, to connect the dots for an audience. We could walk those scenarios from start to finish and talk about what the consequences could be, and educate on how this specific risk is mitigated or combatted. One might then extend it further to the future extrapolated super intelligence scenario, where this risk is not necessarily human orchestrated.

However it might make more sense to just start communicating focused on the risks that are still extreme but not existential, like consolidation of wealth and power.

If you tell someone "there's a 10% chance that the plane will crash" they have a clear picture in their head of what that catastrophe might look like from start to finish.

If we say "AI has an X% chance of ending humanity" they just imagine 'robots take over'; it is too easy to dismiss. Even if it's true and well intended.

Given what recently happened I started asking myself about the future of ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) in days of AI. I refer to recent publications on advances in solving Millenial problems coming from OpenAI and Anthropic.

Please keep in mind : Bitcoin still uses Secp256k1 for its signatures and public-private key ownership model even today.

Let me summarize Millenial problem #5 : BSD (Birch-Swynnerton-Dyer conjecture)

The Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer (BSD) conjecture is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems in mathematics. It concerns elliptic curves over the rational numbers and connects two apparently different kinds of information: the rational points lying on an elliptic curve and the analytic behavior of a function called its L-function.

1. Rational points on an elliptic curve

An elliptic curve over the rationals can be written, in a simple form, as

    E: y² = x³ + ax + b,

with rational coefficients and nonzero discriminant. We are interested in solutions (x,y) whose coordinates are rational numbers. These rational points form an abelian group under a geometrically defined addition law.

The Mordell–Weil theorem says that this group has the form

    E(Q) ≅ E(Q)_tors ⊕ Z^r.

The integer r is called the rank. It measures the number of independent rational points needed to generate the infinitely recurring part of the group.

2. The L-function

For each prime p, one can count the number of points of the curve over the finite field F_p. For a good prime, define

    a_p = p + 1 − #E(F_p).

These numbers are assembled into an Euler product defining the elliptic-curve L-function L(E,s). Thus the L-function encodes a large amount of arithmetic information about the curve, obtained from its behavior modulo primes.

3. The central BSD prediction

The key claim of BSD is that the rank of the elliptic curve can be read directly from the order of the zero of its L-function at s = 1:

    rank(E(Q)) = ord_(s=1) L(E,s).

For example, if L(E,1) is nonzero, BSD predicts rank 0. If L(E,1)=0 but L′(E,1) is nonzero, it predicts rank 1. If the first nonzero derivative is the second derivative, it predicts rank 2, and so forth.

4. The stronger statement

BSD goes beyond the rank. It predicts a precise formula for the leading nonzero Taylor coefficient of L(E,s) at s=1. This formula involves deep arithmetic invariants of the elliptic curve, including its regulator, periods, torsion subgroup, Tamagawa numbers, and the Tate–Shafarevich group Sha(E).

The conjecture therefore links analytic data from an L-function with detailed algebraic information about rational solutions.

5. Why it matters

The conjecture is remarkable because it proposes a bridge between geometry, number theory, finite-field computations, and complex analysis. The rational-point problem can be extremely difficult: even knowing that rational points exist does not necessarily reveal the rank. BSD predicts that the same information is encoded in the behavior of L(E,s) near one specific point, s=1.

Please ❤️like, 🔖bookmark, and 🔁share with fellow growth stock traders/investors

In this Short Insights video from our podcast recorded on Sep 4, @Jacksonneidich highlights $DELL and $HPE as two of the strongest technical setups within the AI infrastructure trade at the time.

Fast-forward to today, and $DELL was down roughly 5% while $HPE was down around 6% — a useful reminder that even the strongest-looking setups still have to prove themselves through price.

*

$DELL stood out because it had built a 14-week base while holding its rising 10-week moving average throughout a period when much of the AI trade was getting hit hard.

That 10-week MA is one of the key “guiding lights” in the O’Neil/CAN SLIM process.

The goal isn’t simply to own whatever AI stocks have the best story — it’s to identify companies with strong fundamentals that are also holding rising 10-week and 50-day moving averages and outperforming the broader market.

At the time, $DELL had passed those tests.

*

$DELL was breaking through $500 to new all-time highs on what looked like roughly 300% of average weekly volume, while its relative-strength line was also pushing to new highs.

Price, volume and relative strength were all pointing toward leadership.

For anyone who missed the initial breakout, Jackson highlighted the 5-week EMA as an important level to watch.

The strongest Stage 2 leaders often respect that average as they advance, meaning a constructive retest around $500 or slightly below could potentially offer another entry — assuming the breakout continued to hold.

*

$HPE was the other standout.

It had developed a textbook cup with a high handle, with the handle forming in the upper half of the base.

After initially gapping down on earnings, $HPE produced what looked like a powerful shakeout and reclaimed the 65-day, 50-day and shorter-term moving averages in one move.

That was a major contrast with earlier climactic reversals that had suggested the stock needed more time to build its base.

Massive volume on the shakeout plus a stochastic hook higher added to the constructive setup.

We initiated a small position in $HPE, with the intention of scaling only if price produced constructive upside confirmation.

And that last point matters.

A great setup is not a guarantee.

*

This analysis shows exactly why price confirmation and risk management remain critical even when fundamentals, relative strength, volume and technical structure appear to line up.

At the time, $DELL looked like the confirmed leader and $HPE like the developing breakout candidate. Today’s sharp declines put both setups under a very different test.

Markets constantly provide new information — and when price changes, your assessment has to change with it.

Would I let an AI agent spend money from my account today?

Probably not.

Sending the payment is not the scary part.

The scary part is letting AI decide what it should pay for, which balance it should use and whether the information it has about me is even true.

Now look at what @PulsarMoneyApp and @verona_dev  are building together.

Pulsar is a money app with USD and EUR balances, stablecoin funding, transfers, swaps and a virtual card.

It also has an AI companion, and later that companion will be able to do more than just show you what happened with your money.

It will be able to act.

And before an agent starts spending, it needs context it can trust.

Imagine you have cash and loyalty points.

The agent wants to buy something for you.

Are those points actually yours?

Did you already buy this product somewhere else?

Do you already pay for this subscription?

Maybe you bought running shoes months ago and have been logging runs ever since. A brand now has a reward specifically for runners.

The agent should not guess any of this.

Verona can turn those facts into proofs.

You choose what to verify and share.

The agent gets the answer it needs without getting all the raw data behind it.

And Pulsar points are also planned to work like something you can actually prove you own, rather than just a number stored in Pulsar’s database.

So an agent could eventually compare:

> use my points
> use my USD balance
> use my EUR balance
> skip the purchase because I already have it

and make that decision using verified information.

Pulsar already wants AI agents to handle routine money tasks, and it is even working on scoped virtual cards where an agent can have its own spending limits and permissions.

You don’t need AI to know everything about you.

You need it to know the right facts when it is about to do something important.

Especially when that something involves your money.
